drug_name: Penicillin G Benzathine / Penicillin G Procaine
what_its_for: This medicine is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections, including strep throat, pneumonia, and some skin infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It is NOT used for viral infections like the common cold or flu.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) into your muscle, usually in the buttock area. It is always given by a doctor, nurse, or other trained healthcare provider in a medical setting — you will NOT give this shot to yourself at home. You will feel a small amount of pressure or discomfort at the injection site, which is normal. Stay in the clinic for at least 10 to 15 minutes after your shot so staff can watch for any allergic reactions.
dosing: Your dose depends on your age, weight, and the type of infection being treated. Your doctor or nurse will decide the right dose for you. Most people receive one injection, but some conditions may require more than one shot or a series of shots given days apart. Always follow your healthcare provider's exact instructions.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given in a clinic, missing a scheduled appointment is the same as missing a dose. If you miss or need to reschedule your appointment, call your doctor's office as soon as possible to set up a new time. Do not skip doses, as this can allow the bacteria to keep growing and may make your infection harder to treat.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home. It is kept in the clinic refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It must never be frozen. Your healthcare team handles all storage for you.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you have ever had a serious allergic reaction to any penicillin or cephalosporin antibiotic before receiving this medicine. Avoid rubbing or massaging the injection site right after the shot. Do not skip any follow-up appointments, as completing your full course of treatment is very important even if you feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you have any of the following after your injection: difficulty breathing or swallowing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, severe dizziness or fainting, rapid or irregular heartbeat, hives or a widespread rash, severe pain, numbness, or discoloration in the leg or area near the injection site, or any feeling that something is very wrong. Also call your doctor if your infection does not seem to be improving within a few days, if you develop diarrhea that is severe or bloody, or if you have any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Because this medicine releases slowly into your body over time, it may take a few days before you notice improvement in your symptoms. Some people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days. Make sure to keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can confirm the infection is clearing up.
special_populations: Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose is based on body weight and will be carefully calculated by your child's doctor. Pregnant women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Penicillin is generally considered safe during pregnancy, but your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks for you. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of penicillin may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Older adults and people with kidney problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. People with allergies: Always tell your healthcare team about ALL your drug allergies before receiving this injection.
